title: Endocrine System — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Hormones lecture (Prof Fay): classification, signaling and steroidogenesis

questions.stem: What distinguishes endocrine secretion from exocrine secretion?

options.label: A
options.text: Release only into a glandular duct

options.label: B
options.text: Release only onto an epithelial surface

options.label: C
options.text: Release to blood or interstitial fluid

options.label: D
options.text: Release only inside a cell nucleus

options.label: E
options.text: Release directly into a synaptic cleft

questions.why: Endocrine cells usually release hormones into interstitial fluid, from which they enter blood and reach distant targets. Exocrine glands deliver their products through ducts or directly to an epithelial surface.

notes.A: Ductal delivery is characteristic of exocrine secretion, such as pancreatic enzyme release into the gut.
notes.B: Release onto an epithelial surface is a route for exocrine products such as sweat or mucus.
notes.D: Nuclear receptors can receive hormonal signals, but nuclei are not the route by which hormones are secreted.
notes.E: Release into a synaptic cleft is local neurotransmission, distinct from hormone delivery by the circulation.

questions.stem: Why does the same circulating hormone affect some organs more strongly than others?

options.label: B
options.text: All cells have identical hormone receptors

options.label: D
options.text: Hormones are active only near the gland

questions.why: Cells respond to a circulating hormone when they express a receptor that recognises it and can couple to a signal. Different receptor levels and downstream pathways can produce different responses.

notes.B: Receptor expression varies between tissues and helps define which organs respond to the hormone.
notes.C: Hormones reach many tissues through capillaries and interstitial fluid rather than acting only on cells in the vascular wall.
notes.D: Endocrine signals can act far from their source if they reach cells with the appropriate receptors.
notes.E: Capillary delivery is widespread. Specificity depends on which tissues express the relevant hormone receptor.

questions.stem: Which combination governs the magnitude of a hormone-induced target-cell response?

options.label: A
options.text: Hormone level, organ size and blood group

options.label: B
options.text: Receptor number, pH and blood colour

options.label: C
options.text: Membrane size, urea level and temperature

options.label: D
options.text: Hormone level, receptor number and affinity

options.label: E
options.text: Cell shape, ATP level and capillary length

questions.why: Hormone concentration and receptor affinity together influence the fraction of receptors occupied. The number of receptors and their coupling to signalling machinery then shape the response.

notes.A: Hormone level matters, but organ size and blood group do not replace receptor abundance or affinity in determining binding.
notes.B: Receptor number matters, but blood colour does not govern occupancy or signalling by hormone receptors.
notes.C: Temperature or urea can influence cells in particular contexts, but neither captures hormone concentration or receptor binding affinity.
notes.E: ATP may be required downstream, but the listed factors do not account for specific binding of hormone to its receptor.

questions.stem: Why can thyroid hormones affect many tissues whereas ACTH targets relatively few tissues?

options.label: A
options.text: ACTH is secreted only into adrenal ducts

options.label: C
options.text: Thyroid hormone travels without blood flow

options.label: D
options.text: ACTH is immediately destroyed by all cells

options.label: E
options.text: Thyroid receptors occur only in thyroid tissue

questions.why: Thyroid hormone receptors are expressed in many tissues, allowing widespread effects on gene expression and metabolism. The main physiological targets of ACTH are selected adrenal cortical cells expressing its functional receptor.

notes.A: Pituitary ACTH travels through blood to the adrenal cortex rather than being secreted into an adrenal duct.
notes.C: Thyroid hormone circulates in blood, largely bound to carrier proteins.
notes.D: ACTH has a limited duration of action, but is not destroyed immediately by all cells.
notes.E: Thyroid hormone receptors are distributed in many target tissues, including tissues outside the thyroid gland.

questions.stem: Which tissue is recognized as an endocrine organ through its production of metabolic signaling substances?
questions.why: Adipose tissue releases circulating signalling proteins called adipokines, including leptin and adiponectin. These connect energy stored in fat to regulation of appetite, metabolism and other functions.

notes.A: The stratum corneum consists largely of terminally differentiated cells that provide a protective barrier.
notes.B: Tooth enamel is a highly mineralised material rather than a living endocrine tissue.
notes.C: Vitreous humour is a transparent gel that supports the shape and optical function of the eye.
notes.D: Mature erythrocytes carry oxygen and do not possess a secretory core specialising in metabolic hormones.

questions.stem: Which process is a principal integrated function of hormones?
questions.why: Hormones coordinate growth and development across tissues. Growth hormone and thyroid hormone are examples of signals that regulate processes extending well beyond the cells that secrete them.

notes.A: DNA replication depends on replication machinery and is not a universal function of endocrine hormones.
notes.B: Fibrin is cleared by fibrinolysis mediated by plasmin, a process distinct from the endocrine control of development.
notes.D: Blood oxygen is carried mainly by haemoglobin in erythrocytes rather than by albumin or hormones.
notes.E: Hormones can influence immune activity, but supply of new antigen receptors is not a general endocrine function.

questions.stem: Which hormone is classically classified as a glycoprotein rather than a simple peptide?
questions.why: FSH is a glycoprotein hormone with noncovalently associated alpha and beta subunits and attached carbohydrate. Its beta subunit helps determine receptor specificity.

notes.B: ADH is a nine-amino-acid peptide hormone that regulates water balance.
notes.C: Glucagon is a peptide from pancreatic alpha cells rather than a carbohydrate-bearing pituitary heterodimer.
notes.D: Oxytocin is a nine-amino-acid peptide involved in uterine contraction and milk ejection.
notes.E: Insulin is a peptide hormone with disulphide-linked chains rather than a classical glycoprotein hormone.

questions.stem: Which hormone is an amino-acid-derived catecholamine?
questions.why: Epinephrine, also called adrenaline, is a catecholamine synthesised from tyrosine through intermediates including dopamine and noradrenaline. It belongs to a different chemical class from adrenal steroids.

notes.A: Aldosterone is a mineralocorticoid synthesised from cholesterol in the adrenal cortex.
notes.B: Progesterone is a steroid and a precursor in other steroidogenic pathways.
notes.C: Testosterone is an androgen derived from cholesterol rather than a catecholamine derived from tyrosine.
notes.E: Cortisol is a cholesterol-derived glucocorticoid from the adrenal cortex.

questions.stem: Which hormone is a cholesterol-derived steroid?
questions.why: Aldosterone is synthesised from cholesterol in the adrenal zona glomerulosa. Its fused-ring structure and the pathway that produces it define it as a steroid.

notes.A: Glucagon is a pancreatic peptide hormone made by processing a protein precursor.
notes.C: Prolactin is an anterior pituitary protein hormone that signals through a cell-surface receptor.
notes.D: Calcitonin is a peptide secreted by thyroid parafollicular cells.
notes.E: Oxytocin is a small peptide made by hypothalamic neurons and released from the posterior pituitary.

questions.stem: Which class of chemical messenger generally requires cell-surface receptors because it does not diffuse readily through lipid membranes?
questions.why: Peptide hormones are generally polar and do not readily cross the lipid bilayer. They bind cell-surface receptors that convey the signal to intracellular effectors.

notes.A: Steroid hormones are lipophilic and classically regulate transcription through intracellular receptors.
notes.B: Thyroid hormones use specific transporters to enter cells and act mainly through nuclear receptors.
notes.C: Retinoic acid is a vitamin A derivative that signals through intracellular nuclear receptors.
notes.D: Calcitriol is a lipid-soluble vitamin D metabolite whose classical receptor is intracellular.

questions.stem: Which immediate target-cell response can be produced by some hormones without new protein synthesis?

options.label: B
options.text: Formation of a new endocrine gland

options.label: C
options.text: Opening or closing membrane ion channels

options.label: D
options.text: Synthesis of a complete cell nucleus

options.label: E
options.text: Replication of the entire cell genome

questions.why: Some hormone signals change the activity of ion channels already present in the membrane. Modulation of their opening can therefore change membrane permeability before new proteins are made.

notes.A: Chromosomal replication is used before cell division, rather than to alter existing membrane permeability rapidly.
notes.B: Formation of a gland requires tissue development, which is much slower than channel gating.
notes.D: Changing a channel's activity uses pre-existing proteins and does not require assembly of a nucleus.
notes.E: Genome duplication is a cell-cycle event, rather than an immediate response required for hormone signalling.

questions.stem: Which intracellular component converts ATP into cAMP after suitable G-protein signaling?
questions.why: Adenylyl cyclase converts ATP into cyclic AMP and pyrophosphate. In the classical stimulatory pathway, active Gs alpha increases the activity of this membrane-associated effector.

notes.B: Phosphodiesterases break down cyclic AMP rather than making it from ATP.
notes.C: Phospholipase A2 releases fatty acids from phospholipids and does not cyclise ATP.
notes.D: Guanylate kinase converts GMP to GDP using a phosphate donor, rather than producing cyclic AMP.
notes.E: A protein phosphatase removes phosphates from proteins. It does not generate cyclic AMP.

questions.stem: In a typical stimulatory G-protein pathway, what is the role of extracellular hormone?

options.label: C
options.text: It acts as the effector enzyme

options.label: D
options.text: It serves as the first messenger

options.label: E
options.text: It binds to newly synthesized DNA

questions.why: The extracellular hormone is the first messenger because its binding initiates signalling through the receptor. The pathway then generates cAMP inside the cell as a second messenger.

notes.A: Adenylyl cyclase catalyses conversion of ATP to cyclic AMP. The extracellular hormone acts by binding a receptor.
notes.B: The first messenger is the extracellular ligand, whereas calcium can be an intracellular second messenger in some pathways.
notes.C: The effector enzyme is adenylyl cyclase, which responds to the activated G protein.
notes.E: A typical hormone in this pathway acts through a membrane receptor rather than by binding newly synthesised DNA.

questions.stem: Which signaling protein couples activated membrane receptors to adenylyl cyclase?
questions.why: A stimulatory heterotrimeric G protein couples receptors to adenylyl cyclase. After the receptor activates it, its GTP-bound alpha subunit stimulates the cyclase.

notes.A: Ribosome-bound tRNA delivers an amino acid during translation, rather than coupling a membrane receptor to an effector.
notes.C: Histone octamers package nuclear DNA in nucleosomes. They do not relay this extracellular signal.
notes.D: ATP synthase makes ATP using an ion gradient rather than communicating receptor activation to the cyclase.
notes.E: Collagen fibres support the extracellular matrix and have no role as intracellular GTP-dependent signal relays.

questions.stem: What occurs to the guanine nucleotide on a stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit when its receptor activates it?
questions.why: Receptors promote GDP release and GTP binding; subsequent GTP hydrolysis helps terminate G-protein activity.

notes.A: GTP serves as the activating ligand on the G protein. The cyclase uses ATP to make cAMP.
notes.B: The bound GDP is released and replaced by GTP rather than being converted to an adenine nucleotide.
notes.C: ATP and ADP are adenine nucleotides, whereas G proteins bind guanine nucleotides.
notes.D: Cyclic AMP is formed downstream of G-protein activation rather than being converted to ATP on the alpha subunit.

questions.stem: What is a principal immediate intracellular target of cAMP signaling?
questions.why: cAMP binds the regulatory subunits of protein kinase A and frees its catalytic subunits to phosphorylate targets. This can rapidly alter the activity of existing proteins.

notes.A: Lysyl oxidase is an extracellular cross-linking enzyme rather than an immediate intracellular cAMP effector.
notes.B: Plasminogen activation is a proteolytic step in fibrinolysis and is not direct activation by cAMP.
notes.D: Histone synthesis is regulated in the context of chromatin and the cell cycle rather than being the immediate cAMP target here.
notes.E: Collagen cross-linking occurs outside the cell and is initiated by lysyl oxidase.

questions.stem: A hormone induces phosphorylation of intracellular regulatory enzymes via cAMP. Which sequence best explains it?
questions.why: Ligand binding activates a receptor coupled to Gs, whose alpha subunit stimulates adenylyl cyclase. Increased cAMP then activates protein kinase A to phosphorylate intracellular targets.

notes.B: Arrestin can reduce receptor signalling and plasmin degrades fibrin, so neither supplies the classical cAMP relay.
notes.C: Collagen is structural and rhodopsin is a visual receptor. This combination does not connect a stimulatory hormone receptor to PKA.
notes.D: Lysine and retinol are not the canonical intermediates that generate cAMP in this pathway.
notes.E: DNA ligase joins DNA ends and thrombin acts in coagulation. The cAMP pathway uses neither as its cyclase effector.

questions.stem: A receptor activates phospholipase C. Which membrane phospholipid is cleaved to produce IP3 and DAG?
questions.why: Phospholipase C hydrolyses phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate on the cytoplasmic membrane face. The products are soluble inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate and membrane-associated diacylglycerol.

notes.A: Dipalmitoyl phosphatidylcholine is a phosphatidylcholine species, without the phosphorylated inositol head group required to release IP3.
notes.B: Phosphatidylethanolamine has an ethanolamine head group and cannot supply inositol trisphosphate.
notes.C: Phosphatidylserine contains serine rather than the inositol group required for this signalling reaction.
notes.E: Sphingomyelin has a sphingolipid backbone and does not yield IP3 and diacylglycerol through this pathway.

questions.stem: Which intracellular effect follows binding of IP3 to its receptor?

options.label: A
options.text: Calcium synthesis from ATP in cytosol

options.label: D
options.text: Conversion of DAG to free cholesterol

options.label: E
options.text: Direct transcription by IP3 in the nucleus

questions.why: IP3 diffuses through the cytosol and binds IP3-gated calcium channels in the endoplasmic reticulum. Opening these channels releases stored calcium into the cytosol.

notes.A: Calcium is an element supplied by existing pools or entry from outside the cell. ATP cannot be converted into it.
notes.C: IP3 receptors are calcium-release channels on the endoplasmic reticulum rather than plasma-membrane sodium channels.
notes.D: DAG remains associated with the membrane and can activate PKC. IP3 does not convert it to cholesterol.
notes.E: IP3 is a second messenger that can alter gene expression indirectly, rather than acting as a transcription enzyme.

questions.stem: Which second messenger activates protein kinase C in the canonical PIP2 pathway?
questions.why: Diacylglycerol stays in the plasma membrane after PIP2 cleavage. It recruits or activates conventional and novel PKC isoforms, with conventional isoforms also requiring calcium.

notes.A: IP3 increases cytosolic calcium from intracellular stores, while DAG is the membrane lipid signal that engages these PKC isoforms.
notes.B: cGMP can activate protein kinase G rather than serving as the membrane-bound PKC signal in this pathway.
notes.C: Pyrophosphate is released in various biosynthetic reactions and is not the lipid messenger from PIP2.
notes.D: Glutathione participates in cellular redox control rather than acting as the DAG-dependent PKC signal.

questions.stem: Which regulatory protein forms a calcium-dependent signaling complex with cytosolic calcium ions?
questions.why: Calmodulin binds calcium at its EF-hand motifs and changes conformation. The calcium–calmodulin complex can then regulate enzymes including calmodulin-dependent kinases.

notes.A: Fibrinogen is a plasma clotting substrate converted to fibrin by thrombin.
notes.B: Transferrin transports iron in blood and is not an intracellular calcium sensor of this kind.
notes.D: Albumin can bind calcium in plasma, but does not relay changes in cytosolic calcium to calmodulin-dependent enzymes.
notes.E: Tropocollagen is a structural collagen molecule rather than a soluble intracellular calcium sensor.

questions.stem: A phospholipase C inhibitor prevents production of IP3 and DAG. Which early response would be impaired?
questions.why: Phospholipase C normally generates IP3 from PIP2. Blocking this step leaves less IP3 to open calcium channels in the endoplasmic reticulum, reducing the early calcium signal.

notes.B: Direct steroid membrane entry does not require production of IP3 or DAG.
notes.C: Vitamin K-dependent carboxylation is a separate enzyme reaction in protein maturation.
notes.D: Translation elongation uses ribosomes, tRNAs and elongation factors, rather than depending directly on production of IP3.
notes.E: Plasmin breaks down fibrin through proteolysis, independently of IP3-mediated calcium release.

questions.stem: What is the common biosynthetic precursor of adrenal glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids?
questions.why: Adrenal steroidogenesis begins with cleavage of the cholesterol side chain to form pregnenolone. Branches of this shared pathway generate glucocorticoids and mineralocorticoids.

notes.A: Glutamate participates in amino acid metabolism and does not provide the intact steroid ring system.
notes.B: Palmitate is a fatty acid rather than the direct shared steroidogenic substrate.
notes.C: Tryptophan supplies precursors for serotonin and melatonin, rather than adrenal steroid rings.
notes.E: Glycine participates in other biosynthetic pathways, including haem synthesis, rather than being cleaved into pregnenolone.

questions.stem: Which product is generated by cleavage of the cholesterol side chain early in steroidogenesis?
questions.why: Cholesterol side-chain cleavage enzyme CYP11A1 acts in mitochondria to form pregnenolone. This is the common first conversion leading towards the steroid hormones.

notes.A: Aldosterone is produced by a later mineralocorticoid pathway, not by the initial cleavage reaction.
notes.C: Cortisol is produced after several additional modifications in the glucocorticoid pathway.
notes.D: Oestradiol is generated later by aromatisation of a suitable androgen precursor.
notes.E: Androstenedione is a downstream androgen and is not formed directly from cholesterol.

questions.stem: Which adrenal cortical region lacks significant 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity and produces aldosterone?
questions.why: The outer zona glomerulosa expresses aldosterone synthase and lacks appreciable CYP17A1 activity. This enzyme profile directs steroid precursors towards aldosterone rather than cortisol or adrenal androgens.

notes.A: The zona fasciculata has 17-alpha-hydroxylase activity and primarily makes glucocorticoids such as cortisol.
notes.B: The zona reticularis has CYP17A1 activity and is an important source of adrenal androgens.
notes.C: The adrenal medulla produces catecholamines rather than aldosterone.
notes.D: The posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin, which are synthesised in hypothalamic neurons.

questions.stem: Which adrenal cortical zone primarily produces cortisol?
questions.why: The zona fasciculata has the enzyme complement needed for glucocorticoid synthesis. Its principal glucocorticoid product in humans is cortisol, released in response to ACTH.

notes.A: The zona glomerulosa is specialised for aldosterone synthesis rather than producing most cortisol.
notes.B: The adrenal medulla secretes catecholamines such as adrenaline.
notes.D: The renal cortex contributes to renin release and other functions but is not the principal site of cortisol production.
notes.E: The posterior pituitary releases hypothalamic peptide hormones rather than adrenal steroids.

questions.stem: What biochemical characteristic allows steroid hormones to cross the plasma membrane readily?
questions.why: Steroids have a relatively lipophilic ring structure, which allows them to partition into and cross the lipid bilayer. This gives them access to intracellular receptors.

notes.B: Extensive charged phosphate groups would limit simple diffusion across the hydrophobic membrane core.
notes.C: A peptide backbone typically makes a hormone more polar, favouring signalling through a cell-surface receptor.
notes.D: Steroids can partition into the bilayer and do not generally depend on crossing through a porin.
notes.E: Permanent ionisation decreases lipid solubility rather than explaining simple steroid diffusion.

questions.stem: Which direct intracellular event commonly follows binding of a steroid hormone to its receptor?

options.label: B
options.text: Direct creation of cyclic AMP from ATP

options.label: C
options.text: Hydrolysis of membrane PIP2 by hormone

options.label: E
options.text: Immediate assembly of a spindle apparatus

questions.why: Classical steroid receptors are ligand-regulated transcription factors. Hormone binding allows the receptor to change transcription at target regulatory regions, often by recruiting other proteins.

notes.A: Extracellular fibrin is formed by cleavage of fibrinogen by thrombin, a separate coagulation reaction.
notes.B: Cyclic AMP is generated by adenylyl cyclase, which is not the classical direct target of a steroid receptor complex.
notes.C: Phospholipase C hydrolyses PIP2 in a different signalling pathway. The steroid hormone itself is not that enzyme.
notes.E: A mitotic spindle is a cell-division structure rather than a general direct product of steroid receptor activation.

questions.stem: Why do many steroid-hormone effects develop more slowly than ion-channel responses to peptide hormones?

options.label: A
options.text: They require synthesis of new cholesterol cells

options.label: B
options.text: They often require altered gene expression

options.label: D
options.text: They operate only through transducin GTPase

questions.why: Many steroid effects depend on changing transcription and then accumulating new proteins. A receptor that changes the activity of an existing ion channel can respond much sooner.

notes.A: The receiving cells can respond to circulating steroid without forming any new cholesterol-producing cells.
notes.C: Extracellular proteolysis is not required for the classical nuclear steroid receptor mechanism.
notes.D: Transducin acts in phototransduction rather than being the obligatory GTPase for steroid receptors.
notes.E: Fibrin polymerisation is a clotting event and not a prerequisite for steroid-regulated transcription.

questions.stem: Which hypothalamic hormone initiates the central stimulation of cortisol release during stress?
questions.why: Hypothalamic CRH stimulates pituitary corticotrophs to secrete ACTH. ACTH then acts on the adrenal cortex, linking the central stress signal to cortisol release.

notes.A: Thyrotropin-releasing hormone primarily stimulates pituitary TSH secretion and drives the thyroid axis.
notes.B: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone stimulates pituitary LH and FSH secretion in the reproductive axis.
notes.C: Growth hormone-releasing hormone stimulates growth hormone release rather than starting the cortisol pathway.
notes.D: Prolactin-inhibiting hormone is dopamine, which restrains prolactin secretion.

questions.stem: Which pituitary hormone directly stimulates adrenal cortical cortisol secretion?
questions.why: ACTH from the anterior pituitary stimulates steroidogenesis in the adrenal zona fasciculata. This increases cortisol synthesis and secretion.

notes.A: TSH acts primarily on the thyroid to increase thyroid hormone production.
notes.B: FSH targets the gonads, supporting ovarian follicle development and spermatogenic function.
notes.D: LH stimulates gonadal steroidogenesis and ovulation, rather than directly driving adrenal cortisol production.
notes.E: Melanocyte-stimulating hormone acts chiefly through melanocortin receptors involved in pigmentation and other functions, while ACTH stimulates cortisol production.

questions.stem: Rising plasma cortisol normally reduces both CRH and ACTH secretion through what mechanism?

options.label: A
options.text: Negative feedback at hypothalamus and pituitary

options.label: C
options.text: Direct calcium removal from target tissues

questions.why: Cortisol inhibits CRH release in the hypothalamus and ACTH release at the anterior pituitary. The resulting fall in stimulatory drive limits further adrenal cortisol secretion.

notes.B: Feed-forward stimulation would reinforce the signal, rather than reducing CRH and ACTH as cortisol rises.
notes.C: Cortisol feedback depends on receptor signalling and does not work by extracting calcium from tissues.
notes.D: Reversible regulation of hormone secretion does not require destruction of adrenal receptors.
notes.E: Pancreatic sympathetic output is not the feedback route linking elevated cortisol to reduced CRH and ACTH.

questions.stem: Which organ is a major site of steroid-hormone inactivation and conjugation before excretion?
questions.why: The liver metabolises many circulating steroids and conjugates them with glucuronide or sulphate. These more water-soluble products can be eliminated in urine or bile.

notes.A: The spleen is important in blood filtration and immunity rather than being the main organ for steroid conjugation.
notes.B: The thymus supports T-cell development rather than handling most systemic steroid inactivation.
notes.C: The retina metabolises some signalling compounds locally but is not a major site of systemic steroid clearance.
notes.E: Bone marrow chiefly supports blood-cell production rather than hepatic-type clearance and conjugation of steroids.

questions.stem: Which hormone principally supports renal sodium retention and potassium excretion?
questions.why: Aldosterone activates mineralocorticoid receptors in distal nephron cells. It increases sodium reabsorption and supports potassium secretion by regulating epithelial transport proteins.

notes.A: Cortisol is primarily a glucocorticoid, and local metabolism in the aldosterone-sensitive nephron normally limits its action on mineralocorticoid receptors.
notes.C: Glucagon regulates fuel availability, especially through actions on the liver.
notes.D: Melatonin carries information about circadian timing and does not chiefly regulate renal potassium secretion.
notes.E: Prolactin chiefly supports milk production rather than acting as the main renal sodium-retaining hormone.
